title: Living Abroad
description: Ten essays, profiles, interviews and personal columns about living in another country: a teacher in Japan, an engineer in Ohio, a family's year in Spain, culture shock, learning a language as an adult and coming home again.

lessons.title: The Invisible Rules
lessons.summary: An American teacher in a small Japanese town learns the rules that nobody writes down.
lessons.text:
Emily Carter, a teacher from Oregon, writes about her first months in Japan.

When I arrived in Japan, I thought the hardest part would be the language. I had a pocket dictionary and a translator app on my phone. What I had not expected was that the most important rules would be invisible. Nobody wrote them down, because everybody already knew them.

My school was in a provincial town of about 30,000 inhabitants, two hours by train from the nearest large city. Like many provincial towns, it was quiet. Most of the inhabitants had lived there all their lives, and very few of them had ever met an American. On my first morning, I walked into the teachers' room in my street shoes. Nobody said anything. Then the vice principal came over, smiled and gently pointed at a row of indoor shoes by the door. Every teacher, I realized, had a pair of indoor shoes, and so did every student. Outside shoes stayed outside. It was the first invisible rule I learned.

For the first few weeks, I was anxious almost all the time. I was anxious about bowing too much or too little and about using the wrong word. Not only did I worry about making mistakes, but I also worried that nobody would tell me when I made them. My dictionary could tell me what a word meant, but it could not tell me when to use it. The translator on my phone was surprisingly good with menus and street signs, but it was no help when a colleague answered a question with a long, quiet pause.

What helped me most was a teacher named Ms. Sato, who had studied in Canada for a year and remembered how it felt to be new in a country. Every Friday, she would gently explain one thing that I had noticed that week. A pause, she told me, often conveys more than words. It can mean "I disagree," or "I need time to think," or simply "This is difficult to say." A small gift conveys thanks without a speech.

Surprisingly, once I understood a few of these invisible rules, the town began to feel less foreign. I stopped checking my dictionary every five minutes. I learned to wait during a pause instead of filling it. The inhabitants, who had seemed so reserved at first, turned out to be warm, curious and very patient with my mistakes.

I still have my indoor shoes, which I wear at home in Oregon too. They remind me that every place has rules that nobody sees, and that learning them is part of the pleasure of living somewhere new.

Questions:
Where did Emily teach English?
She taught in a provincial town in Japan of about 30,000 inhabitants.
What was the first invisible rule she learned?
She learned that everyone wears indoor shoes inside the school and that outside shoes stay outside.
Why was Emily anxious in her first weeks?
She was anxious about bowing and using the wrong word, and she worried that nobody would tell her about her mistakes.
What could the dictionary and the translator not do?
They could not tell her when to use a word or what a colleague's pause meant.
What did Ms. Sato explain about pauses?
She explained that a pause often conveys more than words and can mean several different things.
How did the town feel once Emily understood a few invisible rules?
It began to feel less foreign, and the inhabitants turned out to be warm, curious and patient.

lessons.title: An Engineer in Ohio
lessons.summary: A profile of a Brazilian engineer who builds a new life, part by part, in a small Ohio town.
lessons.text:
When Rafael Souza left São Paulo four years ago, he had never seen snow. Today he lives in a small town in Ohio, where he works as an engineer for the American subsidiary of a Brazilian company. The subsidiary has its own factory, with about 400 workers, who manufacture compact electric motors for washing machines, fans and small farm machines.

Rafael's job is to make sure that every motor they manufacture works exactly as it should. He calculates how much heat each motor will produce, tests new configurations of parts and looks for defects before the motors leave the factory. Last year, his team found a configuration that made the motors quieter and even more compact. "A defect that costs one dollar to fix here can cost a thousand dollars when it reaches a customer," he explains. "So we calculate everything twice."

He was sent to Ohio as the successor to an older Brazilian engineer, Marcos Lima, who was retiring after twenty years abroad. Marcos showed his successor how the factory worked, but he also gave him advice that had nothing to do with motors. "Buy a good winter coat in October, not in December," he said. "Learn the names of your colleagues' children. And find a hobby that gets you out of the house."

The last piece of advice took the longest. In Brazil, Rafael's hobby had been playing soccer on the beach with friends every Sunday. In Ohio, the nearest beach was hundreds of miles away, and for several months of the year the fields were covered in snow. During his first winter he stayed at home and felt, as he puts it, "like a motor running without a machine."

Things changed when a colleague invited him to join an indoor soccer league that played every Wednesday evening in a school gym. Within a few weeks, his old hobby had given him a group of friends and a nickname, "the Professor," because of the careful way he calculates every pass.

This year, Rafael has a new role: he welcomes the incoming engineers who arrive from Brazil each year. Before they arrive, he sends every incoming engineer a list that looks very much like the one Marcos once gave him. He has only added the schedule of the indoor league.

"The factory is the easy part," he tells them. "Motors follow rules. A new life does not. You have to build it slowly, part by part, test it and fix the defects as you find them."

Rafael still misses the beach, and his mother still calls every Sunday to ask whether he is warm enough. But when people ask him where home is, he no longer needs to calculate the answer. "Home is here," he says, "and also there."

Questions:
Where does Rafael work, and what does the factory manufacture?
He works for the Ohio subsidiary of a Brazilian company, which manufactures compact electric motors.
Why does his team calculate everything twice?
A defect that costs one dollar to fix in the factory can cost a thousand dollars when it reaches a customer.
Whose successor was Rafael?
He was the successor to Marcos Lima, an older Brazilian engineer who was retiring.
How did Rafael return to his old hobby?
A colleague invited him to join an indoor soccer league that played every Wednesday evening.
What does Rafael do for the incoming engineers?
He welcomes them and sends each of them a list of advice, like the one Marcos once gave him.

lessons.title: The Four Stages of Culture Shock
lessons.summary: An essay describes the four usual stages of culture shock and asks how useful the idea really is.
lessons.text:
Anyone who moves abroad is likely to hear about culture shock, usually during an orientation session in the first week. The idea is that people who move to a new culture tend to pass through several stages of feeling. Most orientation programs describe four.

The first stage is one of excitement. Everything is new and interesting. The new arrival enjoys the vibe of the city and writes home about how friendly everyone is. At this stage, people rarely grasp the complexity of the place they have moved to. They see the surface, and the surface is charming.

The second stage begins when the excitement fades. Small problems begin to plague daily life: a bank form that nobody can explain, a bus that never comes. The new arrival starts to grasp how much they do not understand, and many people feel tired and lonely. Long periods of stress raise the level of a stress hormone in the body, and too much of this hormone makes it harder to sleep.

The third stage is adjustment. Slowly, the new arrival learns the rules, makes a few friends and finds routines that work. The problems that plagued them in the second stage become easier to handle. Their outlook changes, too. Instead of asking, "Why are things here so strange?" they begin to ask, "Why are things done this way here?"

The fourth stage is acceptance. The person does not stop noticing differences, but the differences no longer feel like a threat. The vibe of a city that once seemed so foreign now simply feels like home. Many people even feel that their outlook has evolved in a way that would not have been possible if they had stayed where they were.

How useful is this model? On the one hand, it gives people a map. Knowing that the difficult second stage is normal, and that it usually passes, can make it easier to bear.

On the other hand, real life is rarely so simple. The model itself has evolved over the years, and researchers point out that people do not move through the stages in a straight line. Some skip the first stage completely; others return to the second stage every winter. The threshold at which a small problem becomes a real crisis is different for everyone. It depends, perhaps most of all, on whether a person has friends nearby.

What the model cannot capture, then, is the full complexity of a human life. But it does not need to. Its value lies less in its accuracy than in its comfort. When a new arrival reaches the threshold of the difficult stage and thinks, "Something is wrong with me," it helps to know that thousands of people have stood at the same threshold before, and that most of them found their way through.

Questions:
What do people fail to grasp in the first stage?
They rarely grasp the complexity of the place they have moved to.
What problems plague daily life in the second stage?
Small problems, such as a bank form that nobody can explain or a bus that never comes, plague daily life.
How does a person's outlook change in the third stage?
They stop asking why things are so strange and begin to ask why things are done this way.
Why is the model not always accurate?
People do not move through the stages in a straight line, and the threshold at which a problem becomes a crisis is different for everyone.

lessons.title: Is It Too Late to Learn a Language?
lessons.summary: An essay weighs the belief that adults cannot learn a new language well against the experience of two adult learners.
lessons.text:
It is one of the most common beliefs about language learning, and people who move abroad as adults hear it all the time: children learn languages easily, while adults struggle. Is it true? The honest answer is that it is partly true, and that the part that is true matters less than most people think.

There is good evidence for the common view. Several influential studies have found that people who begin a language in early childhood are far more likely to sound like native speakers. If an adult starts learning at forty, the probability that he or she will one day have a perfect accent is low.

However, the same research supports a second, more hopeful stance. Adults learn many parts of a language faster than children do. They already understand how grammar works, and they can study on purpose. An adult who studies thoroughly for a year may know more words than a child who has lived in the country for the same year. In other words, adults may not reach a comparable accent, but they can reach a comparable level of understanding.

More importantly, the goal of most adult learners is not a perfect accent. It is to live, work and make friends in a new language. For that goal, other things seem to matter more than age: how much time a person spends with the language and whether they are passionate about it.

Consider two learners. Ana moved from Mexico to Toronto at the age of 38. She was passionate about English long before she arrived. She learned the words of songs by her favorite rapper, and she could repeat them faster than her teenage son. Peter, an American, moved to France at 55. He studied French grammar thoroughly every morning, but what really helped him was a French comedian whose shows he watched every evening. To understand the jokes, he had to understand not only the words but also the culture behind them.

After three years, both of them speak with an accent, and both of them have jobs, friends and opinions in their new languages. What they share is not a special talent. It is that each of them found something in the language that they truly enjoyed, a rapper for one and a comedian for the other, and returned to it every day. Pleasure may be the most influential thing of all, because it keeps people going during the slow months.

So, is it too late? If learning a language means sounding exactly like someone born in the country, then for most adults the probability is low, and it is better to accept that early. But if it means understanding, being understood and, most importantly, building a life, then my stance is clear: it is never too late. An accent is not a failure. It is simply a sign that you have come from somewhere, and that you have chosen to arrive.

Questions:
What have several influential studies found?
They have found that people who begin a language in early childhood are far more likely to sound like native speakers.
What is the goal of most adult learners?
Their goal is not a perfect accent but to live, work and make friends in the new language.
How did Ana learn English?
She was passionate about English and learned the words of songs by her favorite rapper.
What helped Peter most with French?
A French comedian whose shows he watched every evening helped him most.
What is the writer's stance at the end?
The writer's stance is that it is never too late.

lessons.title: Our Year in Spain
lessons.summary: An American mother remembers her family's sunny year in a small town near Valencia.
lessons.text:
Last August, my husband, our two children and I moved from Chicago to a small town near Valencia, in Spain. My husband, David, had a year away from his university, and we decided that the whole family would go with him. Now that the year is over, I want to write down what it gave us before the memories fade.

Our apartment was on the top floor of an old building with blue and white tiles on the stairs. The tiles in the kitchen were painted with oranges and lemons, and our daughter, Lily, who was 8, gave each of them a name. Behind the building was an orange grove, and in March, when the trees were in flower, the whole street smelled sweet. Every Sunday we walked through the grove to a small white chapel on the hill. The chapel was cool and quiet, and the old man who looked after it always showed the children something new.

The children went to local schools, and at first they went separately: Lily to the primary school and Max, who was 13, to the secondary school across town. For the first month, they came home separately too, both tired and a little sad. By November, however, they were translating for us at the market.

The market was my favorite place. Every Saturday the vendors set up their tables in the main square, and within a few weeks I knew most of them by name. The fruit vendor, a friendly woman called Pilar, always gave Lily a free orange "for the road."

Most days were sunny, even in winter, which still amazes someone from Chicago. On sunny weekends we went to the beach, where the water stays shallow for a long way out. Lily could walk far from the shore with the water only up to her knees, and in the shallow water she found small fish and shells.

In May, we took a boat trip, and about two miles from the shore we saw dolphins. There were five or six of them, jumping beside the boat as if they were showing off. Max, who had spent most of the year pretending to be bored, stood at the front of the boat and shouted, "Fabulous! Fabulous!" Later he said that the dolphins were the best thing about the whole year. Lily disagreed. For her, the best thing was Pilar's oranges.

On our last evening, we climbed the hill to the chapel and watched the sunset over the grove. The sunsets there are long and golden, and the light turns the white walls pink. David held my hand, Max took photos of the sunset, and Lily said goodbye to the trees one by one.

We are back in Chicago now, and the children are speaking English again. But in our kitchen there is a single blue tile, a gift from the old man at the chapel, and every morning it reminds us of a fabulous year.

Questions:
Where did the family walk every Sunday?
They walked through the grove to a small white chapel on the hill.
Why did the children go to school separately?
They went separately because Lily went to the primary school and Max went to the secondary school across town.
What did the fruit vendor always do?
She always gave Lily a free orange "for the road."
What did Lily find in the shallow water?
She found small fish and shells.
What did the family see from the boat, and what did Max shout?
They saw five or six dolphins, and Max shouted, "Fabulous!"

lessons.title: Twenty Years as a Host Family
lessons.summary: In an interview, a host mother in Minnesota talks about pillows, pets and the students who became family.
lessons.text:
For twenty years, Linda and Mark Olson have welcomed exchange students into their home in Minnesota. In that time, 23 students from 14 countries have lived with them, each for a school year.

How did you become a host family?

Our nephew spent a year with a host family in Norway when he was 16, and he came back more confident and more curious. Mark and I thought that if a family in Norway could do that for our nephew, we could do the same for someone else's child.

What is the first thing you do when a new student arrives?

I show them their room, and I give them a choice of pillows. People sleep on very different pillows around the world. One girl from Korea wanted a small, firm pillow; a boy from Italy wanted three soft ones. So the pillow comes first.

Is it difficult for students to fit into family life?

Sometimes. We are a big clan. On holidays there might be thirty people in our house, all talking at once. For a quiet student, the whole clan can be too much. I tell them it is fine to dodge the noise for a while and go to their room. After a few months, most of them stop dodging and start arguing about football with the uncles.

Do students ever expect something different?

One boy, years ago, had watched too many movies. I think he expected a big house with a butler. On his first evening, Mark showed him how to load the dishes. The boy laughed and said, "So I am the butler." He turned out to be the best butler we ever had.

Tell us about the pets.

We have a dog, Pepper, and a cat, Opal. Pepper loves everyone immediately. She will lick a new student's hand before they are through the door, and lick their face if they let her. Opal is suspicious of strangers. Every year she stays suspicious for about two weeks and watches the new student from the top of the stairs, and then one evening the suspicion is gone and she is asleep on their bed.

Have you ever had a funny misunderstanding?

A few years ago, we hosted a girl from Japan named Hana. On Halloween night, our neighbor's son jumped out from behind a tree dressed as a clown and shouted, "Boo!" Hana screamed, then looked at me with deep suspicion, as if I had planned it. I explained that people shout "boo" to scare each other as a game. By the end of the evening, she was saying "Boo!" to every child who came to the door. Mark, who loves to play the clown, was delighted.

What have you learned from twenty years of hosting?

That people are more alike than different. Every student misses home at some point, and every student cries at the airport. We were delighted to be invited to three of their weddings, in Brazil, Germany and Korea. They are part of the clan now.

Questions:
Why did Linda and Mark become a host family?
Their nephew came back from a year in Norway more confident and more curious, and they wanted to do the same for another child.
Why did one boy expect a butler?
He had watched too many movies.
How do the two pets welcome new students?
Pepper licks their hands right away, but Opal is suspicious of them for about two weeks.
What happened to Hana on Halloween night?
A boy dressed as a clown shouted "Boo!" and she screamed, but later she was saying "Boo!" herself.

lessons.title: Coming Home a Stranger
lessons.summary: A woman returns to Wisconsin after seven years in Korea and slowly learns to live with two homes.
lessons.text:
Sarah Moore taught English in Korea for seven years. Here she writes about coming home.

I came back to Wisconsin last spring. Everyone warned me about culture shock when I left. Nobody warned me about culture shock when I came back.

At the airport, all the announcements were in English, which should have been a comfort. Instead, it felt almost unbelievable to understand every word around me without trying. For seven years, the conversations of strangers had been a pleasant background noise. Now I heard every word, and, unbelievable as it sounds, I could not switch it off.

Then there was the house. I grew up in an ordinary house on an ordinary street, but in my memory it had become something close to a mansion, with a huge kitchen and a yard as big as a park. When I walked in, the whole place seemed to have shrunk. The house had not really shrunk, of course. My memory had turned it into a mansion, and my apartment in Korea, which was about the size of my parents' garage, had changed my idea of space.

The harder part was people. My oldest friends were kind and glad to see me, but our conversations felt strangely hollow. They asked about Korea, listened for two minutes and then changed the subject. It is difficult to imagine a life you have never seen. Still, their questions sounded hollow, and so did my answers, as if we were all reading from a script. I had expected our friendships to continue where they had stopped. Instead, I worried that they might fracture under the weight of everything we could not share.

There was also a void where my other life had been. In Korea, I had a routine: my Thursday language class, my morning walk in the park. At home, that whole life simply disappeared, and nothing filled the void. I felt like a stranger in my own town.

What helped was nothing dramatic. I ditched the idea that I had to choose between my two homes. I also ditched the habit of starting every sentence with "In Korea, we..." Then I joined a Korean cooking class at the community center, and the teacher turned out to be a woman from Korea who missed her country as much as I now missed it. Our conversations were intimate, because we did not need to explain anything to each other.

Slowly, my old friendships healed rather than fractured. One friend asked me to teach her to cook a simple Korean soup, and over that soup we had the most intimate talk we had had in years.

I have come to see my confusion as a testament to how much the years abroad changed me. If coming home had been easy, it would mean that I was still the same person who left. Those hard months were a testament to growth. Like most growth, it hurt for a while and then made room for something new.

Questions:
What surprised the writer at the airport?
It felt almost unbelievable to Sarah to understand every word around her without trying.
Why did the house seem to have shrunk?
Her memory had turned it into a mansion, and her small apartment in Korea had changed her idea of space.
Why did conversations with old friends feel hollow?
Her friends listened for only two minutes and then changed the subject, as if everyone were reading from a script.
What is her confusion a testament to?
It is a testament to how much the years abroad changed her.

lessons.title: Review: Far From Home
lessons.summary: A review of a small museum's exhibition about the immigrant miners who built a Pennsylvania borough.
lessons.text:
Small museums rarely receive much attention, but the new exhibition at the historical museum in Westvale, a borough of about 6,000 people in Pennsylvania, deserves a visit from anyone who is interested in how immigrants helped to build America.

A borough, for readers outside Pennsylvania, is a small town with its own local government, and Westvale was once a typical coal borough. Between 1880 and 1920, thousands of miners came here from Wales, Italy, Poland and Ireland. They worked underground for twelve hours a day, and in the evening they returned to small timber houses that the mining company had built for them. "Far From Home" tells their story through objects, letters and art.

The first room shows the inside of one of those timber houses. There is a narrow bed, a table and an iron stove that a miner's wife would stoke with coal early every morning, long before the sun came up. Beside the stove hangs a tin bucket, and on the table lies a tin lunch box, old and scratched, which belonged to a 14-year-old Polish miner named Jan Nowak. It is a simple object, but it is hard to look at it without thinking about the boy who carried it every day.

The most notable part of the exhibition, however, is its art. In the second room hang thirty paintings by Anna Russo, a painter whose grandfather was an Italian miner in Westvale. Russo spent three years talking to the families of the borough's miners, and her paintings show their stories: a wedding in a timber church, a mother stoking the stove, children playing in the snow beside the mine. The painter works in warm brown and gold colors, and although her style is simple, her people are full of life.

At the center of the last room stands a sculpture by a local artist, made from old timber taken from a mine that closed in 1962. The sculpture shows a miner and his wife standing side by side, each holding a lamp. It is not a large sculpture, and it is not a perfect one, since the faces are rough and the bodies are a little too long, but it is the most moving piece in the exhibition. Visitors leave notes at its base, many of them from the families of Westvale's miners.

The exhibition has a few weaknesses. Some of the labels are too long, and the story of the women who cooked and cleaned for the miners deserves more space. But these are small complaints. "Far From Home" is a notable achievement for a museum of this size, and a warm tribute to the people who crossed an ocean to dig coal in the dark and who, in the process, made a new home in a small Pennsylvania borough.

Questions:
What is a borough in Pennsylvania?
A borough is a small town with its own local government.
Where did Westvale's miners come from, and where did they live?
They came from Wales, Italy, Poland and Ireland, and they lived in small timber houses built by the mining company.
What is in the first room?
There are a narrow bed, a table, an iron stove, a tin bucket and a tin lunch box that belonged to a young Polish miner.
Who is Anna Russo?
She is a painter whose grandfather was an Italian miner in Westvale.
What does the sculpture in the last room show?
It shows a miner and his wife standing side by side, each holding a lamp.

lessons.title: Kenji's Studio in Lisbon
lessons.summary: A profile of a Japanese massage therapist who has made a home in Lisbon.
lessons.text:
Kenji Mori has lived in Lisbon for eleven years, and he has a simple way of describing his job. "People come to me tight," he says, "and they leave loose." Kenji is a massage therapist from Osaka. His small studio, two rooms above a café, is booked for weeks ahead.

He came to Portugal almost by accident. In his twenties, he worked at a busy massage clinic in Osaka, where he sometimes gave ten massages a day. On a vacation in Lisbon, he fell in love with the city's light, its hills and its slow afternoons. Six months later he had sold his car, packed two bags and moved.

The beginning was not easy. He spoke no Portuguese, and he had no clients. To find them, he left small cards in cafés and shops. Many of his first clients were older people who still had phones with a dial. "They would dial my number, wrap the phone cord around their fingers and talk for twenty minutes before they asked about the price," he remembers, laughing. "It was good practice for my Portuguese."

Today his clients include office workers, dancers and tour guides, and many of them have the same problem: a painful shoulder. "Look at the strap of your bag," he says. Most people carry a heavy bag with a single strap over the same shoulder every day, for years. Over time, the muscles in the neck become as hard as a cord. Kenji works on them slowly, and at the end of each massage he gives the same advice: move the strap to the other shoulder, or, better still, carry a bag with two straps.

On his day off, Kenji likes to walk along the river to Belém, where great ships once left for distant lands. He often stops at a monument to the explorers of the fifteenth century, among them the admiral Vasco da Gama, who led the first expedition to sail from Europe to India. Kenji finds the story of that expedition moving. "The admiral did not know what he would find," he says. "I felt a little like that when I came here, like a small expedition of one person."

Near the monument, older men often fish from the river wall, using worms to catch the fish. Kenji has become friends with several of them. One of them, Rui, who fished for a living for 50 years, taught him how to put a worm on a hook, and in return Kenji gives Rui a free massage once a month. "His shoulders are terrible," Kenji says. "That is what 50 years of pulling nets does."

Asked whether Lisbon now feels like home, he thinks for a moment. "I still eat rice every day, and I still bow when I say thank you," he says. "But I have Portuguese friends, a Portuguese cat and an old friend by the river who saves me the best worms. I think that is a kind of home."

Questions:
What is Kenji's job, and where is he from?
He is a massage therapist from Osaka.
How did his first older clients phone him?
They would dial his number on phones with a dial and wrap the phone cord around their fingers.
What causes many of his clients' shoulder problems?
They carry a heavy bag with a single strap over the same shoulder every day for years.
Who was Vasco da Gama?
He was an admiral who led the first expedition to sail from Europe to India.
What did Rui teach Kenji?
Rui taught him how to put a worm on a hook.

lessons.title: Can You Belong to Two Places?
lessons.summary: An essay weighs both sides of the question of whether a person can truly belong to two countries.
lessons.text:
A short video recently went viral in which a young woman, born in Kenya and raised in Canada, was asked a simple question by a stranger: "Where are you really from?" She smiled and answered, "Both." The video was shared millions of times. Some people found her answer beautiful; others argued that a person has to belong somewhere first.

Can a person truly belong to two countries? The question deserves to be taken seriously from both sides.

Those who have doubts usually make an argument about duty rather than feelings. A country, they say, is not only a culture but also a system of governance: laws, taxes, elections and duties. Citizens share responsibility for that governance, and responsibility, in this view, works best when it is not divided. This is not necessarily a nationalist argument, and many people who make it are warm toward immigrants. But it rests on the idea that a person's first loyalty should be clear.

Those on the other side reply that identity is not a contract with a single country. A man can be a good son and a good father at the same time. In the same way, they argue, a person can feel at home in two places without being less loyal to either. To demand a single answer is to hold people hostage to a choice that does not reflect their lives. No one, they say, should be a hostage to a passport.

Both sides, it seems to me, have a point. It is reasonable to expect people who live in a country to take an active part in its governance: to vote, to follow the law and to care about the people around them. But it is not reasonable to expect them to forget where they came from. Memory is not a lack of loyalty.

What worries me more than either argument is the tone that the debate sometimes takes. In some nationalist speeches, immigrants appear as villains who have come to take something away. In others, people with doubts about belonging to two countries are painted as villains too. Neither picture is fair. Most people on both sides are simply trying to understand how a community holds together.

Perhaps the most useful idea here is tolerance, not in the weak sense of putting up with other people, but in the stronger sense of accepting that other lives turn around a different axis. For some people, life turns around a single fixed axis: one language, one town, one flag. For others, the axis runs between two places, and they travel back and forth along it all their lives. Neither is better. Both are human.

My own plea, then, is a simple one. When we meet someone like the young woman in the viral video, we could ask her a different question. Not "Where are you really from?" but "What do you love about both places?" It is a small plea for tolerance, and for curiosity, which may be the warmest form of tolerance.

Questions:
What happened in the viral video?
A stranger asked a young woman where she was really from, and she answered, "Both."
What does the other side reply?
They reply that identity is not a contract with a single country and that no one should be held hostage to a single choice.
What does the writer mean by tolerance?
The writer means accepting that other people's lives turn around a different axis.
What is the writer's plea?
The writer asks people to replace "Where are you really from?" with "What do you love about both places?"
